---
title: "Criticizing an epidemic model"
description: "Testing the boarding-school SIR fit against its data: posterior predictive checks at two horizons, a negative-binomial observation model, prequential model comparison, and an attack rate that disagrees with the historical record."
camdl-run-scratch: first-fit
---

A fit that converged tells us the sampler found the posterior of the model we
wrote. It does not tell us the model is a good description of what happened.
This page takes the converged SIR fit from [Your first fit](first-fit.qmd) and
asks that second question three ways: by comparing its predictions with the
data it was fitted to, by fitting a competing model and scoring the two, and by
checking an inferred quantity against a number the fit never saw. The first two
point to the same weakness and suggest a repair; the third finds a problem the
repair does not touch.

The commands run in a copy of
[`docs/guide/first-fit/`](https://github.com/vsbuffalo/camdl/tree/main/docs/guide/first-fit),
as on the first page. Each page builds its own fits, so this one starts by
repeating the first page's fit and its predictive check:

```{.camdl-run show-match="converged|max R̂|subsampling"}
camdl fit run fit-r0.toml --label r0 --seed 4
camdl fit predict @r0
```

## Where the Poisson model misses

```{.camdl-run figure="ppc-r0.svg" caption="Posterior predictive check of the Poisson model: median (line), 50% and 90% bands, and the observed counts (black)."}
uv run plot_predictive.py ppc-r0.svg Poisson=results/fits/fit_r0-*/predict/*/
```

The two panels answer different questions. The free-forward band (left)
simulates each epidemic from day 0 using only posterior draws of the parameters,
so it asks whether the model can produce an epidemic like this one. It is wide,
because an epidemic that takes off a day early or late stays early or late, and
13 of the 14 counts fall inside its 90% band. The one-day-ahead band (right)
predicts each day's count from the particle filter's estimate of the epidemic
given the counts before it, so it asks whether the model knows how much a
single day's count can vary. It is narrow, and only 10 of the 14 counts fall
inside it. The misses are all in the decline, where the observed counts first
stay above the model's median and then fall below it: the school's epidemic
ended more abruptly than the model's.

A free-forward check can pass while a one-day-ahead check fails, as here,
because uncertainty about when the epidemic took off dominates the free-forward
band and hides how much any one day may scatter. Both checks test particular
consequences of the model; passing one does not show that the model is right.

Two things could produce the one-day-ahead misses. The observation model may
be too tight, or the SIR dynamics may be wrong in the decline. The first is
easier to test.

## A model that allows noisier counts

A Poisson count has variance equal to its mean. With 300 boys in bed, the model
expects the recorded count to lie within about $\pm 2\sqrt{300}\approx\pm35$ of
the number infected. Counts read off a graph of a school infirmary are unlikely
to be that precise. The negative binomial distribution adds a *dispersion*
parameter $k$, and the observation model becomes

$$
y_t \mid x, \theta \sim \operatorname{NegBin}\bigl(\text{mean} = I_t(x),\ \text{dispersion} = k\bigr),
\qquad
\operatorname{Var}(y_t \mid x, \theta) = I_t(x) + \frac{I_t(x)^2}{k}.
$$

A small $k$ allows much more scatter; as $k\to\infty$ the distribution becomes
Poisson. The process model, and therefore the distribution of epidemics, is the
same as before; only the link from an epidemic to the counts changes.

```{.camdl include="first-fit/sir-negbin.camdl" lines="15-26"}
```

```{.camdl include="first-fit/sir-negbin.camdl" lines="41-48"}
```

The `neg_binomial` distribution's `r` argument is $k$. Its prior is log-normal
with median 20 and 90% of its weight between about 4 and 100. At a mean of 300
boys, that range lets the standard deviation of a count be between about twice
and about nine times the Poisson one, since the ratio is $\sqrt{1 + 300/k}$; at
small counts every $k$ in the range is close to Poisson. `fit-negbin.toml` is
`fit-r0.toml` with the new model and a start value for `k`.

```{.camdl-run show-match="NegBinomial|prevalence|uncommon|point-in-time|converged|max R̂|% ✓|Rhat="}
camdl fit run fit-negbin.toml --label negbin --seed 4
```

The chains converge from the same seed. camdl notes that a negative binomial on
a count of people currently infected, rather than on new cases, is uncommon.
The usual reason to use one is that transmission itself is overdispersed, which
belongs in the process model; here the extra scatter stands for error in how
the counts were recorded and read off the graph, which is an observation
process, so the choice is deliberate.

```{.camdl-run show-match="── posterior" show-context="4"}
camdl fit summary @negbin
```

The two models give nearly the same epidemic. The posterior mean of $R_0$ is
3.73 here against 3.81 for the Poisson model on the first page, and of
$\gamma$ 0.51 against 0.49. The dispersion $k$ has a posterior mean of about
46, above the prior's median of 20: at 300 boys in bed that makes the standard
deviation of a count about $\sqrt{1 + 300/46}\approx2.7$ times the Poisson
one, a modest amount of extra scatter. What differs is how much a day's count may scatter, and the predictive
check shows the consequence:

```{.camdl-run figure="ppc-both.svg" caption="Posterior predictive checks of both models: median (line), 50% and 90% bands, and the observed counts (black)." show-match="subsampling"}
camdl fit predict @negbin
uv run plot_predictive.py ppc-both.svg Poisson=results/fits/fit_r0-*/predict/*/ \
  "Negative binomial"=results/fits/fit_negbin-*/predict/*/
```

The negative binomial's one-day-ahead band is wider and holds 13 of the 14
counts, where the Poisson model's held 10; its free-forward band holds all 14.

## Comparing the two models

`camdl compare` scores each fit by how well it predicts each day's count from
the counts before it. Its headline score is the *expected log predictive
density*,

$$
\mathrm{elpd} = \sum_{t=0}^{13} \log\Bigl(\frac{1}{M}\sum_{m=1}^{M}
  \widehat p\bigl(y_t \mid y_{0:t-1}, \theta_m\bigr)\Bigr),
$$

the total log probability the model gave each observed count before seeing it.
The inner average is over $M = 64$ posterior draws $\theta_m$, each with its
own particle filter, so the score is that of the model's predictive
distribution with its parameter uncertainty included, not of one parameter
value. Higher is better.

```{.camdl-run}
camdl compare @r0 @negbin
```

Each row is a model. `Δelpd` is its elpd minus the baseline's (the Poisson
model, `@r0`), and `se(Δ)` the standard error of that difference across days.
`crps`, the continuous ranked probability score, is an error in boys in bed,
lower being better. `PIT_cov90` is the fraction of days whose count fell inside
the model's one-day-ahead 90% interval.

The difference in elpd is 0.3, with a standard error of 2.2, so the counts do
not prefer either model, and camdl says so (`within noise`). The coverage is
where they differ. The Poisson model's one-day-ahead 90% intervals contain 71%
of the counts, 10 of the 14 days; the negative binomial's contain 93%. The
Poisson model's smaller `crps` does not contradict this. `crps` rewards narrow
predictions and penalizes a miss roughly in proportion to how far off it is,
while the log score penalizes a confident miss much more heavily, so a model
that is usually close and occasionally overconfident can win on one and not the
other.

Fourteen points cannot settle the choice by score alone, and the footer says
why the scores flatter: they are in-sample, because the parameters were fitted
to the same counts being scored, and that favors the more flexible model. Of
the two, the negative binomial is the one to report. It gives the same answer
about the epidemic, and its one-day-ahead intervals contain the counts about as
often as they claim to. Keep in mind how it gets there. The Poisson model's
misses fall in the decline, where the free-forward check showed the model's
epidemic ending too slowly, and the negative binomial covers those days by
allowing more scatter, not by explaining why the decline was faster.

The `ⓘ` lines are informational. `StartsAtPrior` says the first day is
predicted from the model's initial state alone, before the filter has seen any
count. `EssCollapse` says that on one day the Poisson model's particle filter
fell below 100 effective particles, a tenth of its 1000, which happens when a
count is improbable under almost every simulated epidemic: one more sign of the
Poisson model's overconfidence.

::: {.internals title="How much can a score difference over fourteen days be trusted?"}

Less than its standard error suggests, for three reasons, each of which camdl
reports. First, `se(Δ)` treats the fourteen daily differences in log score as
the data, and a normal approximation to their sum is rough with so few. camdl
corrects for the differences being correlated from day to day, and prints the
lag-one autocorrelation it corrected for (+0.25 here), but no correction makes
fourteen days into many. Read `se(Δ)` as a description of scatter, not as a
test. Second, each elpd is itself a Monte Carlo estimate from particle
filters; the `filter-noise MC SE` note puts that noise at a few hundredths of a
unit here, negligible next to the difference. Third, the scores are in-sample,
optimistic by roughly the number of parameters fitted according to the footer,
and the negative binomial fitted one more, so a fair comparison would move
`Δelpd` slightly further against it; the conclusion, no preference either way,
does not change. [Model comparison in camdl](../methods/model-comparison.md)
gives the details, the evidence scale in decibans, and a held-out mode that
scores days the fit did not see.

:::

## What the fit cannot see

The `quantities` block reports, for each posterior draw, `attack_rate`, the
fraction of the school ever infected. `fit predict` wrote its posterior
quantiles for both fits:

```{.camdl-run}
head results/fits/fit_*/predict/*/quantities/attack_rate.tsv
```

Both models infer that nearly the whole school was infected: the posterior
median of `attack_rate` (`q50`) is 97% for the negative binomial and 98% for
the Poisson model, and even the 5% quantiles (`q05`) are 93% and 95%. The BMJ note counts 512 of 763 boys ill, 67%.

The fit had no way to notice. The daily counts record how many boys were in bed,
never how many escaped, and the model reconciles the counts with an epidemic in
which almost everyone was infected. Either about a third of the boys were
infected without falling ill enough to be counted, or the model is wrong in a
way the counts alone do not expose. One candidate is the simplification flagged
on the first page: a boy in the infirmary was isolated, and probably infected
fewer others than an `I` in the model does, which would also explain an
epidemic that ended faster than the model's. Telling those explanations apart
needs data this fit did not use, such as a serological survey or a model with a
separate isolated compartment fitted to the same counts.

This is the strongest check on the page, and the only one that uses
information independent of the fourteen counts. A posterior predictive check
compares the model with the data it was fitted to; an external number can
contradict a model that fits those data well. [The reasoning behind the fit
workflow](../concepts.md#validating-against-the-world) places these checks in
order of strength, and the [fit workflow](../workflow.md) lists what a larger
fit adds.
